quote: Problem den Parallelen Satz in der Ebene ohne Parallelenaxiom zu beweisen, [-?-] [-?-] oder seine Unbewei- sbarkeit zu zeigen
english: The problem of proving the parallel theorem in the plane without the parallel axiom, or of showing its unprovability.
topic: Remarks on models as ends in themselves (citing Fritz Kötter's polemic against Klein–Sommerfeld on numerical computation), an analogy between the quadratic reciprocity law and hydraulic formulas, and a reflection that all thinking consists in finding simpler problems, illustrated by the parallel axiom and the determination of 3-parameter continuous transformation groups.

triage.modern_statement: This is the classical parallel-postulate problem. Using only the other axioms of plane geometry (Euclid's first four postulates, or a modern system such as Hilbert's incidence, order, congruence and continuity axioms), either derive the Euclidean parallel property or prove that it cannot be derived. Proving it cannot be derived means building a model where all the other axioms hold but the parallel axiom fails, such as a model of the hyperbolic plane. Hilbert seems to use it on this page mainly as an example of reducing a problem to a simpler one, not as a new research question of his own.
triage.answered_by: The unprovability side holds. Bolyai and Lobachevsky developed non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) geometry around 1830. Beltrami's 1868 model gave a concrete realization of it, and later Klein and Poincaré models (from the standard history, not checked in this search) made the relative consistency explicit. Hilbert himself treated the independence of the parallel axiom carefully, with model constructions, in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899). That book grew out of his Göttingen lectures of 1894–1898, which is likely the period of this note. Historians disagree on whether Beltrami himself meant his model as an independence proof.

evidence.claim: In 1868 Beltrami gave a concrete realization of Lobachevsky–Bolyai non-Euclidean geometry using the pseudosphere.
The relative consistency of non-Euclidean geometry was proved using models, beginning with Beltrami's 1868 model.
A consistent model of hyperbolic geometry shows that the parallel postulate is logically independent of the other postulates, and independence proofs are usually done by exhibiting such models.
Historical caveat: one author argues that Beltrami in 1868 did not intend to prove consistency or the independence of the parallel postulate.
Hilbert's Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899) was based on his Göttingen lectures of 1894–1898.
Hilbert's Grundlagen shows that its axioms are consistent by giving an arithmetical model for them.

triage.why: The note asks for a proof of the parallel theorem without the parallel axiom, or a proof that this is impossible. That question was settled in the 19th century: the parallel axiom cannot be proved from the others. Models of hyperbolic geometry, starting with Beltrami in 1868, show this relative to the consistency of Euclidean geometry. Hilbert gave his own axiomatic, model-based treatment in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899). It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems; the closest is the 4th problem, which concerns geometries where a straight line is the shortest path between two points. The page context, 'all thinking consists in finding simpler problems,' suggests Hilbert was using the well-known question as an illustration. The two unreadable words keep me from fully ruling out a narrower plane-geometry variant, such as one tied to particular continuity or congruence assumptions.
